html:
Nemo Console, Agent Hub and Engine Console are three local control planes I run every day. All three started as FastAPI backends with a zero-build browser UI. As of this week all three backends are Rust: Nemo Console 0.4.0, Agent Hub 0.3.0 and Engine Console 0.5.0: about 56,000 lines of Python source, counting Engine Console's node agent and Agent Hub's search service.

The reasons were practical. Engine Console's node agent runs on six machines, and a single static binary is easier to put on a DGX Spark than a Python environment. The consoles sit idle most of the day, so start-up time and resident memory matter more than peak throughput. And the security bar these tools need (loopback services that start containers, edit config files and hold keys) is easier to hold with a compiler that refuses unsafe and unwrap.

The constraint was the hard part: nothing may break. Same API, same status codes and error bodies, same settings and file formats, the user's existing database and keys loaded as they are, the same bytes written into other tools' config files, and for Engine Console the same wire protocol, because a Rust hub has to keep driving the Python nodes already installed on remote machines. This post is about how that was checked, and what the checking found.

A contract before any Rust

For each app the first step wrote no feature code. It produced:

  • The route table, dumped from the running Python app, with roles, request bodies and response shapes.
  • A porting contract listing every setting, persisted file format, metric name, subprocess argument list and security control, each control with the Python line it came from and the Rust test that would fail without it.
  • A Rust skeleton with every route already registered. Routes not yet ported answered 501 not_ported, so a missing route could never look like a working one.
  • A test map: one row for every pytest id, 4,508 across the three apps, each to be filled with the Rust test that covers it, or "N/A" with a reason. A row counts as mapped only if it names a real #[test] function; a checker enforces that.

The work was then split into workstreams with disjoint file ownership, each in its own git worktree and branch, and merged with git merge as each one finished. A test that needed another workstream's code was marked #[ignore = "pending WS-X"]. The final gate failed on any such marker, so none could be forgotten.

The referee: run both, compare everything

Unit tests prove what their author thought of. A port also has to match what nobody wrote a test for, so each app got a differential harness: a zero-dependency Node script that starts the Python server and the Rust server one after the other in the same hermetic layout (temp home directory, state seeded by the Python code, fake upstream services, fake command-line tools on PATH), sends both the same requests and compares status codes, chosen headers, normalised JSON, and the files each side wrote to disk.

Two rules made it trustworthy:

  1. Python against Python first. The harness must report zero differences when both sides are Python. That proves the normalisation rules (timestamps, generated ids) hide only genuine noise.
  2. Every difference is either fixed or written down. The allow-list of accepted differences shrank to almost nothing, and the entries that remain still compare the status and body; only a named header may differ.
AppHarness casesResult against the last Python code
Nemo Console1,393 HTTP cases, plus start-up errors and launcher checks1,392 equal, 1 documented deviation
Agent Hub431 hub cases, 114 knowledge-service cases0 differences (a few allowed for extra security headers, and for the adapter added in Rust)
Engine Console674 HTTP steps in three modes, 875 wire-protocol vectors0 differences (9 allowed for extra security headers)

Some properties need more than an HTTP comparison, so each app also got cross-implementation checks:

  • each implementation opens the database and files the other one wrote;
  • for Nemo Console, either launcher's stop stops a console the other one started, and 26 kinds of bad setting give the same exit code and message;
  • for Engine Console, the hub-node protocol in all four combinations against recorded transcripts: Python hub with Rust node, Rust hub with Python node, and both pure pairs.

Every app's existing browser suite, a headless Chrome visiting every page and tab, was pointed at the Rust backend too.

"Exactly like Python" is a long list

Most of the effort went into behaviour nobody thinks of as a feature until it changes:

  • Floats. Python's repr rounds exact ties to even; Rust's formatter rounded them up, so 17 of 9,018 golden values were wrong until the core was fixed. The same bug sat in the JSON and validation-error output.
  • YAML. Agent Hub writes other tools' config files, so its YAML had to be byte-identical to PyYAML 6.0.3: YAML 1.1 booleans (yes, on), the emitter's quoting and line folding, the exact error messages. The answer was a port of PyYAML's pure-Python loader and dumper, about 6,800 lines, checked against a corpus captured from the Python test suite itself and 630,000 comparisons with a live Python oracle on random documents. It is also 25 to 50 times faster than PyYAML on large inputs.
  • TOML. The usual Rust crate parses TOML 1.1; Python's tomllib parses 1.0 and rejects what 1.1 allows. That meant a port of CPython's parser too.
  • Validation errors. FastAPI's 422 bodies come from pydantic's lax coercion rules: which floats count as booleans, how a dictionary key's location is printed. Golden cases generated by pydantic itself pin them.
  • The rest: difflib's matcher with its auto-junk heuristic for plan diffs, fnmatch, shlex, str.isprintable with Unicode 15.1 tables, int() accepting non-ASCII digits, Starlette's Range and ETag handling, prometheus_client's text format, and uvicorn's habit of running start-up work before binding the port.

All of it lives in compatibility layers of roughly 8,000 to 11,000 lines per app, which is the main reason the Rust source is about three times the size of the Python it replaced. Golden files are generated by the Python code, and the generators are committed so the goldens can be rebuilt.

What the port found in the Python code

A second implementation that must agree byte for byte reads the first one more closely than any review. The bugs it found:

  • Three security bugs in Agent Hub 0.2.0, published as GHSA-7j23-gq83-5j4w:
    • the content-migration step followed symbolic links in git metadata, so a planted link could make it delete or overwrite files elsewhere (high);
    • a symlinked .git/config was read and quoted in an error message (medium);
    • the inbox listing accepted a path as its client filter (medium).
  • A data-loss bug in Nemo Console's Data Designer page: once a run's records file reached 2,000 lines, later batches silently dropped out of the user's csv, jsonl and json copies. Rust keeps Python's behaviour until both are fixed together, because a port is not the place to change outputs quietly.
  • A hang. In Agent Hub, a named pipe swapped in at an apply target hung the apply while it held the hub's lock.
  • A clock bug. Nemo Console built run ids from two clock readings, which could sort a new run before an older one at a second boundary.
  • Engine Console's node kept probing engine ports after refusing an invalid policy file, and a policy could make a writable model root overlap the node's own configuration. Both are fixed in the Rust node.

The rule was simple: keep Python's behaviour, record every bug, and break parity only for security.

Tests that reached things they should not

The most uncomfortable findings were about the tests, old and new:

  • Two of the existing browser suites were not hermetic. One sent read-only requests to my live router and routing services on every run. The other read my real GPUs. Both now run against fakes by default, check that before the first page, and need an explicit opt-in to touch anything live.
  • A unit test leaked a key. A ported test copied a default URL that in Python was intercepted by a mocking library. In Rust nothing intercepted it, and the test sent my shell's router key to my own local routing service. Since then, every test default points at a closed port and children get a scrubbed environment.
  • A test passed for the wrong reason. Under my umask, a test's policy file came out group-writable. The node correctly refused it, fell back to a default policy that probes engine ports, and the test still passed because it only checked the mode it reported. Tests now assert that the policy actually loaded.
  • The proof is the whole test suite run under strace -e trace=connect: every connection goes to an ephemeral loopback port. The first CI run on GitHub then caught one more environment leak: a file-mode assertion recorded under my umask, which the runner does not share.

Independent audits

Each port then got an independent review that started with no context: it read the code, not the porting notes or anyone's summary of them. All three came back "ship with fixes", none critical. The same classes appeared in all three, and they are what a Python-to-Rust port loses by default:

  • Limits uvicorn had and a bare Rust server lacks: an idle keep-alive timeout, a header deadline, a connection cap, and a truncated body treated as an error instead of a shorter body.
  • Background loops. Python wrapped each poller tick in try/except; in Rust a panic silently ends the task. The fix catches each tick, redacts the panic message and recovers poisoned locks.
  • Role checks done by hand in each handler, with a test that only read the route table. Roles are now enforced by the request pipeline, and a test calls every route as a viewer and without a key.
  • File and process hygiene: readers that would block on a named pipe, child output buffered without a cap, an interpreter found on PATH (where a user-writable directory comes first), and build paths baked into release binaries.

The numbers

Measured on the same machine, same hermetic setup, release builds, 2,000 sequential requests per route, three interleaved passes (medians):

PythonRust
Cold start to first 200, Nemo / Agent Hub / Engine Console241 / 264 / 272 ms12 / 12 / 9 ms
Knowledge service cold start (LanceDB)659 ms11 ms
Resident memory at idle, the three consoles61–64 MB15–18 MB
Knowledge service memory at idle153 MB22 MB
Nemo /overview p504.5 ms0.66 ms
Agent Hub /doctor p502.0 ms0.32 ms
Engine Console /engines p500.34 ms0.15 ms
Engine Console node agent on a remote machinea Python 3.10+ environmentone 4.7 MB binary

Two routes got slower: Agent Hub's health check, which spawns git on every call and costs more child CPU from Rust, and Engine Console's 580 KB /learn document. Neither was profiled yet. Latency under concurrency was not measured, and on the smallest routes the Rust numbers sit at the measuring client's own floor.

Where it stands

  • Nemo Console 0.4.0 is deployed. With the Rust backend, the browser suite was run once against the real systems (router, routing layer, Dynamo, GPU telemetry, Prometheus, guardrails): all 46 pages and tabs rendered with no error.
  • Agent Hub 0.3.0 runs on my real content repository, with a DeepSeek Harness adapter added along the way.
  • Engine Console 0.5.0 is released with x86_64 and arm64 node binaries. It has passed every comparison against the Python code, but it has not yet run real GPU launches, remote machines or arm64 hardware. Remote machines can move one at a time, since either hub speaks to either node.

Each repository keeps its porting record (backend/PORTING.md): the decisions, every deliberate difference from Python with its reason, and the Python bugs found. The last Python commit stays the reference the parity harness runs against, so any later change can still be compared with the original behaviour.
